A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisEscape and VisEscaper. All 22 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v3, including appendices, tables, figures, and prompts, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations, human gameplay results, memory ablations, and analyses of exploration, captions, and puzzle-solving behavior.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark and human results and adds model evaluations, isolated puzzle experiments, reasoning analyses, and human validation of automated annotations.

M1.justification: V1's Memory, Feedback, and ReAct components correspond to v3's memory management and post-/pre-action reasoning. The corresponding prompts preserve their procedures (v1 Tables 9–13; v3 Tables 16–20). Explicit memory-update timing and expanded game-construction descriptions provide documentation without establishing an algorithm change.

E1.justification: The same 20 rooms and dataset composition remain. V3 Appendix C.2 adds a distinct test scenario using existing puzzles: models receive paired clue and lock images with their relationship specified, replacing exploration and clue discovery with isolated visual question answering.

E2.justification: V3 adds Gemini-1.5-Pro, Gemini-2.0-Flash, and Qwen2.5VL-32B to the reported BaseAgent/VisEscaper and hint-guided comparisons. It removes the Random baseline reported in v1 Tables 2–3. These changes substantially broaden the principal model comparisons.

E3.justification: V3 introduces memory-by-reasoning controls for repetition analysis, counting only object interactions and answer submissions. Its new puzzle protocol tests 20 paired-image problems with and without reasoning at pass@1 and pass@10. Reasoning annotation adds GPT-4o classification and a 500-instance human validation sample. The main gameplay limits and three trials per room remain.

E4.justification: V3 adds analyses of memory–reasoning interaction, normalized trajectory progress, isolated puzzle reasoning, and reasoning composition with human annotation checks. V1's direct memory-removal ablation reporting escape-performance metrics (Table 5) disappears. Existing exploration-memory, brute-force, caption, and hint-progress analyses largely carry over.

E5.justification: V3 Table 13 newly reports step-count standard deviations, described as calculated over successful trajectories; v1 reports means without this variability information. Both versions specify three runs per room. Interpretation is limited by inconsistent entries, including a nonzero standard deviation for InternVL2.5-38B despite its reported zero no-hint success rate.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial model and diagnostic results, including Gemini-1.5-Pro's 25.0% no-hint success rate and reasoning-annotation agreement of 85.6%. Existing values also change: average human duration becomes 318.5 rather than 343.8 seconds. InternVL2.5-38B's image row changes from 3.3% SR/9.02% GC in v1 Table 4 to 0%/6.20% in v3 Table 7, aligning it with v1 Table 3.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results or proofs. The expanded FSM description and reasoning-category explanations do not introduce substantive mathematical reasoning; the existing evaluation metrics retain their meaning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift a principal contribution from proposing a three-module VisEscaper framework toward explaining memory and reasoning in exploration-driven problem solving. Memory–reasoning synergy becomes an explicit central claim. The benchmark contribution and claim that unaided models struggle remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations connecting reduced repetition to memory–reasoning synergy and model differences to hypothesis formation and visual-puzzle reasoning. It also acknowledges that automated reasoning annotations confuse guesses with hypotheses. The limitations concerning real-world generalization and discrete actions remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 adds code/dataset access information, GPT-assisted game-logic construction details and its prompt, explicit backbone-model mappings, memory-update timing, and prompts and settings for the new analyses. Hardware documentation changes from four A6000 or L40S GPUs per large model to two or four A6000 GPUs. These materially expand reproducibility information without demonstrating changes to the retained agent.

R1.justification: New Appendix E explicitly contrasts VisEscape with the previously cited EscapeBench and newly discussed IDEA and MM-Escape. Supporting citations for models, memory, reasoning, and multi-image processing also change. The broader survey of text games, embodied environments, and GUI agents largely retains its scope.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively rewritten and reorganized: benchmark challenges become a separate section, baseline evaluation precedes VisEscaper, related work moves near the end, and module terminology is regrouped. The appendices are substantially reordered and expanded, beyond changes attributable solely to new experiments.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the opening and agent diagrams, adds a construction diagram and analytical plots, and restructures model tables into baseline results, before/after comparisons, and hinted results. Existing plots and puzzle illustrations move to appendices, and human-interface screenshots are combined. These are extensive display and layout changes.

improvement.justification: V3 provides more informative diagnostics of module interaction and puzzle reasoning, broader model comparisons, and substantially better construction and reproducibility documentation. Benefits are tempered by removing v1's direct memory ablation on escape performance and introducing reporting inconsistencies: Section 5.3 calls Qwen comparable to Claude despite Table 3's 3.3% versus 21.7% success rates, and Table 13 contradicts its successful-trajectory restriction. The added insight supports a limited net improvement.
